teaser: Christie's 1934 novel of a murder in a snowbound train car and twelve suspects — the case that forces Poirot to choose between the law and justice. The most ingenious of her locked-room puzzles.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the train and the murder
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the Orient Express is stranded and Ratchett is found dead. Notice how Christie manages twelve suspects without losing the reader. Write what the famous solution says about the relationship between justice and law.

name: Rebecca
teaser: Daphne du Maurier's 1938 novel of the nameless second Mrs. de Winter, the house Manderley, and the dead first wife who still rules it — a Gothic romance about the ghosts of marriage.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the meeting and Manderley
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the narrator marries Maxim and arrives at Manderley. Notice how du Maurier makes the house and Rebecca's absence into characters. Write what 'Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again' promises about memory and haunting.

name: Jamaica Inn
teaser: Du Maurier's 1936 novel of Mary Yellan, sent to her aunt's Cornish inn on the moors — where the landlord runs a wrecking crew and the storms hide worse. A Gothic thriller of wind, dread, and survival.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the journey to the inn
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Mary's ride across the moor and her arrival at the inn set the tone. Notice how du Maurier makes the landscape hostile and alive. Write how the inn's isolation and its secrets feed each other.

name: Orlando
teaser: Woolf's 1928 fantasy-biography of a poet who lives for centuries and changes sex — a love letter to Vita Sackville-West, and the most playful of Woolf's novels. Time, gender, and glory as a game.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the boy and the centuries
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Orlando moves from the Elizabethan court into the centuries. Notice how Woolf treats history as costume and gender as costume. Write what the novel's freedom from biography's rules allows it to say about identity.

name: A Room of One's Own
teaser: Woolf's 1929 essay on women and fiction — the locked library, the imaginary Shakespeare's sister, and the famous claim that a woman needs money and a room of her own to write. The founding text of feminist criticism.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Beadle and the library
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the essay's narrator is turned away from the library and from the grass. Notice how Woolf turns argument into narrative. Write what 'Shakespeare's sister' illustrates about talent and circumstance.

name: A Passage to India
teaser: Forster's 1924 novel of Dr. Aziz, Mrs. Moore, and the Marabar Caves — a friendship across empire tested by accusation and echo. The novel that asked whether connection can survive politics.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mosque and the caves
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Aziz meets Mrs. Moore in the mosque, then read the cave scene. Notice how Forster withholds what happened in the cave. Write what the echo — 'boum' — represents, and why the novel refuses to resolve it.

name: Howards End
teaser: Forster's 1910 novel of the Schlegels, the Wilcoxes, and the house that means England — 'Only connect.' The novel of class, culture, and who inherits the land.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the house and the families
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the connection between the cultured Schlegels and the practical Wilcoxes is established. Notice how Forster turns the house into the novel's conscience. Write what 'only connect' asks of people divided by class.

name: Sons and Lovers
teaser: D. H. Lawrence's 1913 novel of Paul Morel, his coal-miner father, and the mother who claims his soul — the Oedipal novel that scandalized and defined modern English fiction. Class, passion, and the family knot.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mother and the sons
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the marriage of Walter and Gertrude Morel founders and the children become her consolation. Notice how Lawrence renders family feeling with raw intimacy. Write what the novel says about mothers, sons, and the women who come between.

name: Women in Love
teaser: Lawrence's 1920 sequel to Sons and Lovers — two sisters, two men, and the search for a love that is not possession, ending in the Alps. His most philosophical novel, and his most radical.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the wedding and the sisters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Ursula and Gudrun meet Birkin and Gerald. Notice how Lawrence uses the wedding as a stage for his ideas about love and power. Write what the novel proposes love might be, beyond ownership.

name: Lady Chatterley's Lover
teaser: Lawrence's 1928 novel of Constance Chatterley and the gamekeeper Mellors — the most famous banned book of the 20th century, prosecuted for obscenity in 1960, and finally read as the tender novel it is.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the marriage and the estate
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Connie's sterile marriage to the paralyzed Clifford is established. Notice how Lawrence links the body's freedom to the book's politics. Write what the novel's frankness was really arguing against in 1928.

name: The Good Soldier
teaser: Ford Madox Ford's 1915 novel of two couples and nine years of friendship — 'the saddest story' told by the most unreliable narrator in fiction. Dowell's calm confession hides everything it reveals.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the confession begins
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Dowell announces the tragedy and then circles it. Notice how the narrator's omissions are the plot. Write what the novel's technique — telling everything and understanding nothing — says about marriage and memory.

name: Of Human Bondage
teaser: Maugham's 1915 semi-autobiographical novel of Philip Carey, the clubfoot and the artist's life — love for the impossible Mildred, poverty in Paris, and the slow education of the heart. The bildungsroman to end bildungsromans.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the school and the clubfoot
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Philip's disability and his orphanhood are established. Notice how Maugham narrates suffering with cool clarity. Write what Philip learns through his bondage to Mildred — and what the novel's ending forgives.

name: The Razor's Edge
teaser: Maugham's 1944 novel of Larry Darrell, who returns from the Great War and refuses the American dream to seek enlightenment in India — told by a narrator who is Maugham himself. The spiritual quest novel of its era.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the return and the refusal
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Larry's refusal of a career is met with bafflement. Notice how Maugham frames the quest through the society that cannot understand it. Write what the title's 'razor's edge' — the hard path — means in the novel.

name: Brighton Rock
teaser: Greene's 1938 novel of Pinkie, a teenage gangster in Brighton who believes in hell — and of the girl who knows too much. A thriller that is really a novel about damnation and mercy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the pier and the killing
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the murder and Pinkie's world are established. Notice how Greene uses the seaside's gaudy surface against the moral darkness. Write what Pinkie's Catholicism — his certainty of damnation — does to his choices.

name: The Quiet American
teaser: Greene's 1955 novel of Saigon in the early Vietnam years — Fowler the jaded journalist, Pyle the idealistic American, and the woman they both love. The novel that warned about American innocence abroad.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the body in the river
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Pyle's death is revealed and then narrated backward. Notice how Greene uses the love triangle to frame the politics. Write what the novel suggests about good intentions — and why it was hated when published.

name: Burmese Days
teaser: Orwell's 1934 first novel of the British Raj in Burma — the timber business, the club, and the one decent man trapped among racists. The novel that taught Orwell what empire was made of.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the club and the district
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the colonial club's petty hierarchies are established. Notice how Orwell exposes the racism that polite fiction of the time ignored. Write how the novel's firsthand anger shaped everything Orwell wrote later.

name: Down and Out in Paris and London
teaser: Orwell's 1933 memoir of poverty — the Paris kitchens, the London doss-houses, and the tramps' code of the road. The book that taught Orwell how the poor actually live, from the inside.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Paris hotel kitchen
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Orwell works as a plongeur in a Paris hotel. Notice how he reports humiliation with dry precision. Write what the book's sociology of poverty — the tramp, the spike, the casual ward — gave to his later politics.

name: Homage to Catalonia
teaser: Orwell's 1938 account of fighting in the Spanish Civil War — the trenches, the lice, and the betrayal of the revolution by its own allies. The book that made him a socialist and a skeptic of all causes.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the militia and the front
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Orwell joins the POUM militia and experiences the war's strange quiet. Notice how he narrates both the idealism and the absurdity. Write what the May Days in Barcelona taught him about power and truth.

name: The Brave Little Tailor and Other Tales
teaser: The Grimms' fairy tales of the tailor who kills seven flies and conquers giants — along with Rapunzel, Rumpelstiltskin, and the stories that shaped childhood for two centuries. The collected dark magic of the European folk tale.

exploreAction.targetName: A selection of tales, including The Brave Little Tailor
exploreAction.instruction: Read several tales, noticing how the Brothers Grimm preserved the stories' violence and wonder. Write what the tales assume about justice, luck, and the world — and why children have always needed their darkness.

name: The Little Prince
teaser: Saint-Exupéry's 1943 novella of a pilot stranded in the desert who meets a prince from a small planet — a fable about grown-ups, roses, and what is essential. The most translated book in the world after the Bible.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the drawing and the meeting
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the narrator's childhood drawing frames the whole book. Notice how the prince's questions expose the absurdity of adult priorities. Write what the book means by 'what is essential is invisible to the eye.'

name: Night
teaser: Elie Wiesel's 1958 memoir of his boyhood in Auschwitz and Buchenwald — the night his faith died with his father, and the silence that followed. The essential testimony of the Holocaust, in a voice that refuses comfort.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Sighet and the arrival
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the community's denial gives way to the cattle cars and the selection. Notice how Wiesel's spare prose carries the enormity without melodrama. Write what the memoir says about the silence of God and the duty of witness.

name: A Tale of Two Cities
teaser: Dickens's 1859 novel of London and Paris during the French Revolution — resurrection, sacrifice, and the most famous ending in English fiction. The guillotine's shadow over a love story.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the wine cask breaks in the street and the shadows of the era are drawn, then the final pages. Notice how Dickens foreshadows the blood. Write what Carton's sacrifice claims about love and meaning.

name: David Copperfield
teaser: Dickens's 1850 autobiographical novel of David's rise from the blacking factory to the novelist's desk — with Mr. Micawber, Uriah Heep, and the warmth of the first-person. Dickens called it his favorite child.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the factory and the stepfather
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where David's childhood is shadowed by the Murdstones. Notice how Dickens draws on his own hidden past. Write how the first-person voice turns the novel into a search for a place to belong.

name: Hard Times
teaser: Dickens's 1854 novel of the industrial town Coketown and the school of 'facts' — the Gradgrind family raised on statistics, the circus girl Sissy Jupe, and the question of what humans actually need. Dickens's most political novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the schoolroom of facts
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Gradgrind's school demands facts and only facts. Notice how Dickens opposes the circus to the countinghouse. Write what the novel says about education, imagination, and the steam engine's human cost.

name: The Pickwick Papers
teaser: Dickens's 1836 first novel — Mr. Pickwick and his club's comic rambles through England, with Sam Weller's proverbs and the Fleet prison's shadows. The book that made Dickens famous overnight.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the club and the first adventures
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the Pickwick Club's expeditions begin in comedy. Notice how the serial structure keeps each chapter self-contained. Write how the novel's warmth — and its sudden turn to the debtors' prison — shows Dickens's range.

name: Nicholas Nickleby
teaser: Dickens's 1839 novel of Nicholas's fight against his uncle Ralph and the monstrous schoolmaster Wackford Squeers — a serial that attacked Yorkshire boarding schools and championed the underdog.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the family and the school
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the Nickleby family's ruin sends Nicholas to Dotheboys Hall. Notice how Dickens builds the horror of Squeers through comedy. Write what the novel's crusade against child abuse achieved in its own time.

name: Tess of the d'Urbervilles
teaser: Hardy's 1891 novel of Tess Durbeyfield, 'a pure woman' destroyed by a society that will not let her be pure — the seduction, the murder, and the sacrifice at Stonehenge. Hardy's most beloved tragedy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the d'Urberville claim
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the family's false pedigree sets Tess's fate in motion. Notice how Hardy indicts the world rather than Tess. Write what the subtitle 'a pure woman' is arguing against, and how the ending completes the argument.

name: Far from the Madding Crowd
teaser: Hardy's 1874 novel of Bathsheba Everdene, the farm she inherits, and the three men who love her — the shepherd Gabriel Oak, the farmer Boldwood, and the soldier Troy. Hardy's sunniest great novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the meeting on the road
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Gabriel Oak first sees Bathsheba and loses his flock. Notice how Hardy makes the Wessex landscape a character. Write what the title promises about the world the novel explores — and how the love plot tests it.

name: Jude the Obscure
teaser: Hardy's 1895 novel of Jude Fawley, the stonemason who dreams of Oxford — and of Sue Bridehead, with whom he breaks every rule. The novel that ended the Victorian novel, and Hardy's fiction career.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the dream of Christminster
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Jude's longing for the university city is established. Notice how Hardy turns the institutions of class into the novel's villains. Write why the book so scandalized its readers — and what it demands we look at.

name: The Mayor of Casterbridge
teaser: Hardy's 1886 novel of Michael Henchard, who sells his wife at a fair and spends his life paying for it — a tragedy of character, corn markets, and the town that watches. 'Character is fate' made flesh.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the sale at the fair
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the drunken Henchard auctions his wife and wakes to the horror. Notice how Hardy presents the act and its lifelong consequences. Write how the novel's title — the man and the office — frames his rise and fall.

name: Silas Marner
teaser: George Eliot's 1861 novel of the weaver who hoards gold until it is stolen and a child arrives in its place — a fable about what money and love actually buy. Eliot's most perfect small book.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the weaver and the gold
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Silas's wronged past and his miserly present are established. Notice how Eliot makes the gold almost human. Write what the theft and the foundling Eppie teach Silas — and the novel's readers — about what is truly valuable.

name: The Mill on the Floss
teaser: Eliot's 1860 novel of Maggie Tulliver, too clever and too loving for her provincial world — and of the brother who cannot forgive her. The novel of family love and its ruin, ending in the flood.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mill and the children
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Maggie and Tom's childhood in the mill is established. Notice how Eliot grounds the tragedy in the economics of the family. Write what the river and the flood mean, and whether the ending is escape or punishment.

name: Adam Bede
teaser: Eliot's 1859 first novel — the carpenter Adam, the beautiful Hetty, and the infanticide at the heart of the English countryside. Eliot's warmest and most human story, rooted in her own childhood.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the workshop and the village
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the village world of Hayslope is established. Notice how Eliot's realism treats the poorest characters with full dignity. Write how the novel's sympathy — extended even to Hetty's crime — was radical for its time.

name: Romola
teaser: Eliot's 1863 historical novel set in Renaissance Florence — Romola, the scholar's daughter, and her brilliant faithless husband Tito, against the backdrop of Savonarola's city. Eliot's most ambitious book.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Florence and the marriage
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Romola's world of learning and Tito's charm are established. Notice how Eliot reconstructs Florence from its archives. Write what the novel says about the collision of ideals — Savonarola's, Tito's, Romola's — in a real city.

name: Shirley
teaser: Charlotte Brontë's 1849 novel of the West Riding, the Luddite riots, and two very different women — the quiet Caroline and the heiress Shirley, whose name she made a girl's name. Brontë's most social novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mill and the two women
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the mill owners and the workers' unrest are established. Notice how Brontë connects the industrial conflict to the women's restricted lives. Write what Shirley's independence meant in 1849, and why the novel names a new kind of heroine.

name: Villette
teaser: Charlotte Brontë's 1853 novel of Lucy Snowe, who goes alone to a Belgian city and teaches in a girls' school — the loneliest and most modern of Brontë's books, and the one she called her best.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the voyage and the school
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Lucy's solitary journey and her arrival at Madame Beck's school are narrated with cool control. Notice how Brontë withholds Lucy's feelings even as she shows them. Write what the novel's ambiguous ending leaves the reader to decide.

name: Agnes Grey
teaser: Anne Brontë's 1847 novel of a governess's trials in two impossible households — the quietest and most honest of the Brontë novels, and the sharpest portrait of the governess's life in English fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the first post
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Agnes's hopes for her first governess post meet the Bloomfield children's cruelty. Notice how Anne Brontë reports the indignities without melodrama. Write what the novel reveals about the status of the Victorian governess.

name: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall
teaser: Anne Brontë's 1848 novel of Helen Graham, who leaves her drunken husband and earns her own living — the first sustained feminist novel in English, shocking enough that her sister Charlotte suppressed a reprint.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the tenant arrives
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the village's gossip meets Helen's secrecy, then the diary that explains her flight. Notice how Brontë uses the frame to build suspense. Write what the novel risks by defending a wife's right to leave.

name: The Professor
teaser: Charlotte Brontë's 1857 novel, written before Jane Eyre and published after her death — William Crimsworth's years teaching in Brussels. Brontë's first attempt at the story she would perfect in Villette.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mill and the decision
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Crimsworth rejects his brother's mill and sails for the continent. Notice how Brontë's male narrator is cool where her female narrators are fierce. Write how this early novel prefigures Villette — and what changed in between.

name: North and South
teaser: Elizabeth Gaskell's 1855 novel of Margaret Hale, moved from the rural south to the industrial north — where the mill master John Thornton and the striking workers teach her a new England. The industrial novel's masterpiece.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the move to Milton
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Margaret's displacement into the mill town is rendered with exactness. Notice how Gaskell gives both master and worker their arguments. Write what the novel proposes about the possibility of understanding across class lines.

name: Ariel
teaser: Plath's 1965 collection, assembled after her death — Lady Lazarus, Daddy, and the poems that made her a myth. A book of fury, transformation, and language pushed to its breaking point.

exploreAction.targetName: Lady Lazarus and Daddy
exploreAction.instruction: Read Lady Lazarus and Daddy aloud. Notice how Plath's rhymes and repetitions build unbearable pressure. Write what the poems do with anger — how does the speaker transform herself on the page, and what does the myth-making cost?

name: The Poetry of Robert Frost
teaser: Frost's New England poems — The Road Not Taken, Mending Wall, Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening — plain speech with terrible depths beneath. America's most beloved, and least simple, poet.

exploreAction.targetName: A selection of poems, including Stopping by Woods and Design
exploreAction.instruction: Read the famous poems, then a darker one like Design or Out, Out—. Notice how Frost's folksy voice turns suddenly strange. Write what the woods in the snow are really about, and why the speaker has 'miles to go before I sleep.'

name: Four Quartets
teaser: Eliot's 1943 sequence of four meditations — Burnt Norton, East Coker, The Dry Salvages, Little Gidding — on time, memory, and the still point of the turning world. The summit of Eliot's poetry.

exploreAction.targetName: Burnt Norton, the opening section
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Burnt Norton, where the rose garden and the passage of time are established. Notice how Eliot returns to the same images with different music. Write what 'the still point of the turning world' means, and how the poem circles toward it.

name: The Cantos
teaser: Ezra Pound's lifelong epic poem, published in fragments from 1917 to 1969 — a collage of history, economics, Chinese ideograms, and personal fury, 'a poem including history.' Monumental and maddening.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening cantos
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening cantos, where the descent into the underworld and the voyage are established. Notice how Pound cuts between voices, languages, and eras. Write how the poem's fragments enact its argument about civilization's decline.

name: Walden
teaser: Thoreau's 1854 account of two years in a cabin at Walden Pond — economy, solitude, and the deliberate life. The founding book of American nature writing and of every project of voluntary simplicity.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Economy and Where I Lived
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Thoreau itemizes his costs and his reasons. Notice how his ledger-keeping is a philosophy. Write what 'the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation' means, and whether the cabin experiment still speaks to you.

name: Civil Disobedience
teaser: Thoreau's 1849 essay born of a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax — on the duty of the individual against the state. The text that Gandhi and King carried into their movements.

exploreAction.targetName: The full essay
exploreAction.instruction: Read the essay, from the jail anecdote to the closing appeals. Notice how Thoreau's wit carries his radical claims. Write what he means by 'that government is best which governs least' — and how his standard of conscience applies to a citizen today.

name: Self-Reliance
teaser: Emerson's 1841 essay, the sermon of American individualism — 'trust thyself,' the nonconformist, and the wholeness of each soul. The text that every American rebel, from Whitman to the counterculture, was raised on.

exploreAction.targetName: The full essay
exploreAction.instruction: Read the essay, noticing how Emerson's aphorisms accumulate into a worldview. Write what he means by the 'aboriginal self' and by 'whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist.' Where do you agree — and where does the doctrine of self-trust need correction?

name: Nature
teaser: Emerson's 1836 manifesto that launched Transcendentalism — the transparent eyeball, the unity of the soul with nature, and the call to an original relation to the universe. American philosophy begins here.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Emerson describes the woods and the 'transparent eyeball.' Notice how he treats nature as both commodity and teacher. Write what the essay means by 'an original relation to the universe' — and whether we still need one.

name: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
teaser: Montaigne's 1580 invention of the essay — 'I am myself the matter of my book' — three volumes of digression, skepticism, and self-knowledge that taught Europe how to think in prose. The most companionable book ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: Of Cannibals and Of the Education of Children
exploreAction.instruction: Read two essays. Notice how Montaigne wanders from his title and returns by instinct. Write what 'que sais-je?' — what do I know? — asks of the reader, and why his self-portrait still feels like a mirror.

name: Meditations
teaser: Marcus Aurelius's private notebooks, written in Greek while emperor of Rome — the Stoic manual of self-discipline, mortality, and the duty of the moment. A ruler talking to himself, and to us.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One — the debts — and a later book
exploreAction.instruction: Read Book One, where Marcus lists what he owes his teachers and family, then a later book of maxims. Notice how the notebook form lets the philosophy breathe. Write which single precept you would carry into a difficult day, and why.

name: The Republic
teaser: Plato's dialogue on justice, the city, and the soul — the allegory of the cave, the philosopher king, and the question of why be just. The book that founded political philosophy.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One and the allegory of the cave in Book Seven
exploreAction.instruction: Read Book One, where the argument about justice begins, then the cave allegory. Notice how the dialogue keeps the reader arguing. Write what the cave's prisoners and the returning philosopher represent — and whether the philosopher should go back down.

name: Nicomachean Ethics
teaser: Aristotle's lectures on the good life — virtue as a mean, friendship as necessity, and happiness as activity of the soul. The most practical book of philosophy ever written, and the most humane.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One — happiness — and Book Two — virtue
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening books. Notice how Aristotle reasons from what we actually do. Write what his doctrine of the mean — courage between cowardice and recklessness — looks like applied to a real choice you face.

name: Confessions
teaser: Augustine's 400 AD spiritual autobiography — the pear theft, the tears, and 'late have I loved thee' — the first great memoir, and the model for every confession since, sacred or secular.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One and Book Eight — the conversion
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening books, where Augustine examines his infancy and his youth, then the garden scene of his conversion. Notice how the memoir turns memory into prayer. Write what the structure — confessing to God rather than to an audience — does to the story.

name: Summa Theologica
teaser: Thomas Aquinas's 13th-century summa of Christian philosophy — questions, objections, and replies arranged with architectural patience. The great synthesis of faith and reason, still argued with today.

exploreAction.targetName: A question on the existence of God
exploreAction.instruction: Read one question, like the five ways. Notice the method: objections first, then the reply, then replies to each objection. Write how the format itself models honest argument, and assess the strength of one of the 'ways.'

name: Leviathan
teaser: Hobbes's 1651 argument for the social contract — the state of nature as a war of all against all, and the sovereign needed to keep the peace. The book that made the modern state thinkable.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the state of nature
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where Hobbes describes the state of nature and its 'nasty, brutish, and short' life. Notice how rigorously he derives authority from fear. Write what the theory assumes about human nature, and where his premises need testing.

name: Two Treatises of Government
teaser: Locke's 1689 argument for natural rights, property, and the consent of the governed — the philosophical foundation of the American and French revolutions, and of every liberal constitution since.

exploreAction.targetName: The second treatise, on civil government
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters on the state of nature and property. Notice how Locke grounds government in consent rather than conquest. Write how his account of labor and property still shapes arguments about ownership and justice.

name: The Social Contract
teaser: Rousseau's 1762 tract that begins 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains' — the general will, the legislator, and the theory of legitimate authority that both inspired and haunted revolutions.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One, the opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Rousseau dissolves and rebuilds the foundations of society. Notice how compressed and prophetic his sentences are. Write what 'the general will' means, and why the concept has been used for both freedom and tyranny.

name: Common Sense
teaser: Thomas Paine's 1776 pamphlet that turned colonial grievance into the case for independence — written in a style 'calculated for the common reader.' The best-selling American book of its century.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Paine argues from 'simple facts, plain arguments, and common sense.' Notice how he speaks to the reader as an equal. Write what made the pamphlet so persuasive in 1776 — and whether its style still works.

name: Rights of Man
teaser: Paine's 1791 reply to Burke's attack on the French Revolution — a defense of natural rights, republicanism, and the poor, written with a fury that got him tried for treason in England.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Paine answers Burke's defense of inherited privilege. Notice how he treats government as an instrument of the people rather than a mystery. Write what 'the rights of man' meant then, and how far those rights now extend.

name: Dandelion Wine
teaser: Bradbury's 1957 novel of a summer in Green Town, Illinois, in 1928 — Douglas Spaulding's twelve-year-old summer of time machines, magic sneakers, and the bottle that holds the season. The great novel of childhood's summer.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the summer begins
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Douglas's summer is declared and the magical sneakers appear. Notice how Bradbury's prose is drunk on the season. Write what the dandelion wine preserves — and what the novel says about the summer we carry all our lives.

name: Something Wicked This Way Comes
teaser: Bradbury's 1962 novel of two boys and a carnival that arrives at midnight in October — the carousel that reverses age, the mirror maze, and the dark showman. The greatest autumn novel ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the carnival arrives
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the lightning-rod salesman warns the boys and the carnival unloads. Notice how Bradbury makes autumn itself a character. Write what the carnival offers — and what it takes in payment.

name: The Body
teaser: Stephen King's 1982 novella of four boys who walk the railroad tracks to see a dead body — friendship, fear, and the summer that ends childhood. The basis of the film Stand by Me.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the walk begins
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Gordie, Chris, Teddy, and Vern set out on the tracks. Notice how King renders boyhood talk with total fidelity. Write what the journey means to each boy — and what they find, besides the body.

name: The Shining
teaser: King's 1977 novel of the Overlook Hotel, its winter caretaker, and his son who shines — a family trapped with the hotel's history. The novel of addiction, rage, and the haunted places inside a family.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the interview and the closing
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Jack Torrance's past and the hotel's offer are established. Notice how King uses the hotel's emptiness as pressure. Write what the novel says about the monsters a father carries — and what the hedge animals are doing.

name: It
teaser: King's 1986 thousand-page novel of Derry, Maine, and the shape-shifting horror that wakes every 27 years — seven children who fight it, and the adults they become. The great American novel of childhood fear and memory.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the storm and the paper boat
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Georgie's paper boat meets the clown. Notice how King moves between the children's 1958 and the adults' 1985. Write what It — the thing that wears your fear — says about the power of facing childhood terrors together.

name: Misery
teaser: King's 1987 novel of Paul Sheldon, the romance novelist held captive by his 'number one fan' Annie Wilkes — a single-room horror story about writing, obsession, and the reader who loves too much.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the crash and the captivity
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Paul wakes in Annie's house and begins to understand his situation. Notice how King builds horror from one room and two people. Write what the novel suggests about the relationship between writers and their most devoted readers.

name: The Dead Zone
teaser: King's 1979 novel of Johnny Smith, who wakes from a coma with the power to see the future by touch — and the glimpse of a politician that demands the hardest choice. The novel of the gift that is also a curse.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the accident and the awakening
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Johnny's accident and his slow awakening are established. Notice how King treats the power as a medical and moral condition. Write what the novel suggests about knowing the future — and the duty that comes with it.

name: Death on the Nile
teaser: Christie's 1937 novel of luxury river steamer, a honeymoon, and a murder — Poirot among the passengers where everyone has a motive and the jewels are not the only thing at stake. Sunlit, elegant, and perfectly engineered.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the cruise and the announcement
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the passengers board the Karnak and the love triangle is announced. Notice how Christie plants every clue in plain sight. Write how the setting — a boat on the Nile — both isolates the suspects and dazzles the reader.

name: The A.B.C. Murders
teaser: Christie's 1936 novel where the killer writes to Poirot to announce the next victim — a serial killer's alphabetical game that ends with one of the most audacious twists in detective fiction. The A.B.C. Murders.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the first letter
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Poirot receives the letter and dismisses it. Notice how Christie uses the serial structure to expand the form. Write how the killer's vanity — writing to the detective — becomes the key to the solution.

name: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd
teaser: Christie's 1926 novel that outraged and delighted readers — the country-house murder narrated by the doctor, with an ending that changed the rules of detective fiction forever. The book every mystery must answer to.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the village and the murder
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the doctor-narrator establishes the village and the victim. Notice how Christie trusts the reader with all the facts. Write what the solution does to the reader's trust in narrators — and why the twist still works.

name: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold
teaser: Le Carré's 1963 novel that stripped the glamour from espionage — Alec Leamas's last assignment across the Berlin Wall, where every loyalty is a lie. The Cold War novel that ended the era of glamorous spies.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the wall and the fall
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Leamas's last agent dies at the Wall and his descent begins. Notice how le Carré withholds the plan's purpose. Write what 'coming in from the cold' means, and how the ending darkens the whole operation.

name: Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy
teaser: Le Carré's 1974 novel of the mole hunt — George Smiley, retired and humiliated, is recalled to find the Soviet agent inside the Circus. The greatest novel of betrayal in English, and the greatest spy novel of all.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the retirement and the recall
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Smiley's quiet retirement is broken by the mole's trail. Notice how le Carré builds suspense from files and conversations rather than action. Write how the novel's moral fog — everyone compromised — makes the mole hunt so absorbing.

name: Call for the Dead
teaser: Le Carré's 1961 first novel, introducing George Smiley — a quiet civil servant's suicide investigation that opens into betrayal, espionage, and the Berlin Wall's long shadow. The spy novel grew up here.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the inquiry and the suicide
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Smiley's routine interview precedes a death. Notice how the novel moves from domestic inquiry to Cold War machinery. Write what Smiley's quiet competence — his 'humble' craft — offers that heroics cannot.

name: The Honourable Schoolboy
teaser: Le Carré's 1977 novel of Smiley's quiet war against the mole's masters — Jerry Westerby, the journalist and part-time agent, sent into the Far East on a mission that will cost him everything.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Circus after the mole
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the depleted Circus rebuilds and Westerby is recalled. Notice how le Carré widens the canvas to Southeast Asia and the money flows. Write what the novel says about the human cost of the intelligence game.

name: Smiley's People
teaser: Le Carré's 1979 novel that closes the Karla trilogy — a dead Russian emigre's message brings Smiley out of retirement for the final confrontation with his opposite number. The quietest, most perfect ending in spy fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the message and the summons
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the dead man's last request reaches Smiley. Notice how le Carré builds the whole novel on a single phone call. Write what the final chess move — Smiley's and Karla's — reveals about the two men's mirroring.

name: The Night Manager
teaser: Le Carré's 1993 novel of Jonathan Pine, a hotel night manager recruited to infiltrate the arms dealer Richard Onslow Roper — a modern thriller of money, power, and one man's quiet revenge.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the night manager and the dossier
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Pine's hotel life and the leaked dossier are established. Notice how le Carré moves the spy novel into the world of commerce and luxury. Write what the novel suggests about the morality of the arms trade and of revenge.

name: The Constant Gardener
teaser: Le Carré's 2001 novel of Justin Quayle, a quiet diplomat in Kenya whose murdered wife was about to expose a pharmaceutical crime — a thriller that indicts the drug companies with reportorial fury.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the murder and the gardener
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Tessa's death and Justin's garden are established. Notice how le Carré alternates grief with mounting evidence. Write what the novel claims about who profits from the suffering of the poor — and whether fiction can indict them.

name: A Perfect Spy
teaser: Le Carré's 1986 novel, his most autobiographical — Magnus Pym, a lifelong spy and lifelong liar, vanishes and writes the confession of a man made of other people's expectations. The great novel of identity as performance.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the disappearance and the confession
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Pym vanishes and his confession begins. Notice how le Carré moves between Pym's childhood and his double life. Write what the novel suggests about a self built entirely from what others needed — and whether such a man can be found.

name: The Little Drummer Girl
teaser: Le Carré's 1983 novel of Charlie, an English actress recruited to play a role so deep she may not survive it — a Palestinian-Israeli thriller about theater, terror, and the performance of belief.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the audition and the recruitment
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Charlie is approached and tested. Notice how le Carré uses the theater as the model for espionage. Write what the novel suggests about the distance between playing a role and becoming it — and whether Charlie can come back.

name: Animal Farm
teaser: Orwell's 1945 fable of the animals who overthrow their farmer and watch the pigs become the new tyrants — 'All animals are equal, but some are more equal than others.' The perfect political allegory.

exploreAction.targetName: The full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read the novella from the Rebellion to the final scene where the pigs and men become indistinguishable. Notice how the commandments change with each betrayal. Write what the novel says about revolution, power, and the danger of leaders.

name: The Man in the High Castle
teaser: Philip K. Dick's 1962 alternate history of a world where the Axis won the war — divided America under Japanese and Nazi rule, and a novel within the novel that imagines the Allies winning. The book that made counterfactual history a genre.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the occupied Pacific states
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the Japanese-occupied San Francisco is rendered in ordinary detail. Notice how Dick's realism makes the counterfactual world feel lived-in. Write what the novel-within-the-novel suggests about history, fiction, and reality itself.

name: Ubik
teaser: Dick's 1969 novel of a world where the dead are kept in cold storage and the living are assaulted by a reality that keeps degrading — 'I am Ubik.' One of the strangest and most moving novels of reality in question.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the moon base and the half-life
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the psychic business and the reality degradation begin. Notice how Dick makes the reader distrust every scene. Write what the Ubik ads — time-stamped and increasingly desperate — reveal about the novel's true setting.

name: Flowers for Algernon
teaser: Daniel Keyes's 1966 novel of Charlie Gordon, whose IQ is tripled by an experimental surgery — told in his own progress reports as intelligence dawns and then begins to fade. The great novel about what intelligence is for.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening progress reports
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening reports, where Charlie's misspellings and his devotion to his teacher are established. Notice how the prose itself measures his rise and fall. Write what the novel suggests about the relationship between intelligence and happiness — and about how we treat the people we call simple.

name: Stranger in a Strange Land
teaser: Heinlein's 1961 novel of Valentine Michael Smith, raised by Martians and brought to Earth — the counterculture's bible, and the novel that made 'grok' a word. A messiah story that questions everything.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Mike's arrival
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Mike's Martian worldview collides with Earth. Notice how Heinlein uses the outsider to expose the tribe. Write what 'grok' — understanding so complete it becomes part of you — asks of the reader.

name: The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress
teaser: Heinlein's 1966 novel of the lunar colony's rebellion against Earth — narrated by the one-armed computer technician Manuel, with the wisecracking computer Mike at his side. The novel that made libertarian revolution thrilling.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the computer and the rebellion
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Mike the computer becomes self-aware and the plan begins. Notice how Heinlein narrates in a clipped lunar slang. Write what the novel suggests about freedom, taxation, and the price of revolution.

name: Starship Troopers
teaser: Heinlein's 1959 novel of Juan Rico's service in the Mobile Infantry — the most argued science-fiction novel ever written, a war story that treats citizenship as something earned. Loved and hated in equal measure.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the drop and the boot camp
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Rico's enlistment and the first drops are established. Notice how Heinlein alternates battle with political lectures. Write what the novel claims about citizenship, service, and the franchise — and where you disagree with it.

name: I, Robot
teaser: Asimov's 1950 story cycle of the Three Laws of Robotics — the laws that robots cannot break, and the paradoxes that prove them. The book that invented the ethics of artificial intelligence.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening stories — Robbie and the laws
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening stories. Notice how Asimov's robots follow rules that generate dilemmas. Write how the Three Laws still frame real debates about AI safety — and where the laws themselves break down.

name: Childhood's End
teaser: Clarke's 1953 novel of the Overlords, who end war and usher in utopia — and of the next stage of humanity they have come to midwife. A serene, terrifying vision of what evolution might demand.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Overlords arrive
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the golden age under the Overlords begins. Notice how Clarke withholds their appearance. Write what the ending suggests about the price of transcendence, and whether childhood's end is a tragedy or a gift.

name: Timescape
teaser: Gregory Benford's 1980 novel of scientists in 1998 sending a message backward through time to 1963 — tachyons, ecology, and the attempt to warn the past. The hard-science novel that won both major awards.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the message and the receiver
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the two timelines are established — 1963 Cambridge and 1998's collapsing ecology. Notice how Benford makes the physics and the politics inseparable. Write what the novel suggests about whether the past can be saved — and whether it would listen.

name: Dune Messiah
teaser: Herbert's 1969 sequel that refuses to let Paul Atreides enjoy his victory — twelve years into his messianic reign, he sees the trap of prophecy closing around him. The anti-chosen-one novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the emperor's trap
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Paul's prescience has become a cage. Notice how Herbert makes the reader pity a god. Write what the novel argues about charismatic power — why is Paul's victory also his prison?

name: Hyperion
teaser: Simmons's 1989 space epic shaped like The Canterbury Tales — seven pilgrims travel to the Time Tombs, each telling why they must meet the Shrike. A cathedral of science fiction, and the most awarded novel of its decade.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the pilgrims assemble
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the seven pilgrims gather. Notice how each tale carries its own genre — war, love, horror. Write how the frame structure makes the Shrike more terrifying for being unseen, and which pilgrim's tale haunts you most.

name: Dirk Gently's Holistic Detective Agency
teaser: Adams's 1987 novel of the holistic detective who solves crimes by solving the whole universe — time travel, Coleridge, and a sofa on a staircase. The most Dickensian time-travel comedy ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the sofa and the professor
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the sofa on the staircase and the missing professor are established. Notice how Adams ties every absurd thread together. Write what 'holistic detection' means — and how the novel's climax pays off every planted joke.

name: The Long Dark Tea-Time of the Soul
teaser: Adams's 1988 sequel — Dirk Gently investigates a severed head, a Norse god, and a contract that forbids the end of the world. The funniest novel ever written about Norse mythology and airport check-in.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the severed head
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the severed head at the airport and the impossible contract are established. Notice how Adams's absurdity always obeys its own logic. Write what the novel's title — the long dark tea-time of the soul — suggests about its real subject.

name: Good Omens
teaser: Pratchett and Gaiman's 1990 apocalypse comedy — an angel and a demon, both comfortable on Earth, try to stop Armageddon while the Antichrist grows up in an English village. The most fun the end of the world has ever been.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the birth and the swap
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the infant Antichrist is misplaced by accident. Notice how the two authors' voices blend into one deadpan register. Write what the novel suggests about good, evil, and the small decencies that matter more than either.

name: Neverwhere
teaser: Gaiman's 1996 novel of Richard Mayhew, who helps a wounded girl and finds himself invisible to London above — and walking the sewers and rooftops of London Below. A dark fairy tale of the city beneath the city.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the girl and the disappearing life
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Richard helps Door and begins to vanish from his own life. Notice how Gaiman maps London Below onto the real city. Write what the novel suggests about the parts of a city — and of us — that ordinary life refuses to see.

name: Metamorphoses
teaser: Ovid's poem of transformation — Daphne's laurel, Narcissus's pool, and two hundred myths stitched into one river of change. The encyclopedia of classical mythology, told with wit and sorrow.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening books — creation and the first metamorphoses
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening books, where creation gives way to the first transformations. Notice how Ovid treats change as both punishment and poetry. Write what the theme of metamorphosis lets the poem say about desire, power, and the refusal to stay still.

name: Inferno
teaser: The first canticle of Dante's Divine Comedy — the descent through the nine circles of Hell, from the uncommitted to the traitors in ice. The most vivid moral landscape ever imagined.

exploreAction.targetName: Cantos I–V, the entrance and the first circles
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening cantos, where Dante enters the dark wood and passes through the gates of Hell. Notice how each circle's punishment fits its sin. Write what the contrapasso reveals about Dante's sense of justice — and where you would place yourself.

name: Paradise Lost
teaser: Milton's 1667 epic of the fall of man — Satan's rebellion, the war in Heaven, and the expulsion from Eden, written as the poet went blind. The poem that made the devil literature's most magnetic character.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One — the council in Hell
exploreAction.instruction: Read Book One, where Satan rallies the fallen angels in Hell. Notice how Milton's blank verse builds its own music. Write what the poem gains by giving evil the best speeches — and what the epic argues about freedom, obedience, and the uses of grief.

name: A Midsummer Night's Dream
teaser: Shakespeare's comedy of four lovers, a fairy king and queen, and a weaver transformed — the play where the forest's magic untangles the heart's confusions. The most joyful night in the theatre.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One and the final act
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, where the lovers' tangles are set, then the final act with the mechanicals' play. Notice how the fairy magic both mocks and mends the humans' chaos. Write what the play suggests about love's unreasonableness — and why it is best played at night.

name: The Tempest
teaser: Shakespeare's late romance of the exiled magician Prospero and the island he rules — the storm he raises, the spirits he commands, and the forgiveness he finally chooses. The play about art, power, and letting go.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One — the storm and the island
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, where the storm and the island's inhabitants are established. Notice how Prospero controls the play's magic as a playwright controls a stage. Write what Prospero's renunciation at the end — the drowning of his book — suggests about art and power.

name: Othello
teaser: Shakespeare's tragedy of the Moor and his ensign Iago — the handkerchief, the poison of suspicion, and the murder of innocence. The play about race, trust, and the evil of small insinuations.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One and the jealousy scenes of Act Three
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, where Othello's love and Iago's grievance are established, then the scenes where the poison works. Notice how Iago turns Othello's own strengths against him. Write what the play says about the power of suggestion, and about the tragedy of trust betrayed.

name: Sense and Sensibility
teaser: Austen's 1811 first novel of the Dashwood sisters — Elinor's restraint and Marianne's passion, tested by poverty, love, and the weather of feeling. The novel that balances two ways of being alive.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the inheritance and the move
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the sisters' temperaments and their reduced fortunes are established. Notice how Austen stages the argument between sense and sensibility in every scene. Write what each sister teaches the other — and which one you would rather be.

name: Northanger Abbey
teaser: Austen's 1817 novel of Catherine Morland, whose head is full of Gothic novels and who expects the abbey to be haunted — a satire of reading itself, and the funniest of Austen's books.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the heroine who is not one
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Austen introduces Catherine as an unheroic heroine and her novel-bred expectations. Notice how the narrator jokes about fiction even while writing it. Write what the novel says about the difference between stories and life — and why the distinction matters.

name: Mansfield Park
teaser: Austen's 1814 novel of Fanny Price, the poor cousin raised among the Bertrams — quiet, principled, and finally right. Austen's most serious novel, and the one she called the most difficult to write.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Fanny's arrival at the Park
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where shy Fanny is transplanted into the great house. Notice how Austen builds the moral contrast between Fanny's constancy and the household's ease. Write why the novel's quiet heroine is so often contested — and what her steadiness is worth.

name: Lady Susan
teaser: Austen's early epistolary novella of the brilliant, amoral widow Lady Susan Vernon, who schemes through letters with total self-possession — Austen's wickedest heroine, and the book she never published.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening letters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening letters, where Lady Susan's maneuvering begins. Notice how the letter form lets Austen show her schemes and her allies' misreading simultaneously. Write what the novella reveals about Austen's comic cruelty — and why she may have kept it private.

name: The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling
teaser: Fielding's 1749 comic epic of the foundling Tom Jones, expelled from Paradise Hall and sent on the road to London — a laughing, sprawling novel about appetite, honor, and the education of a good heart.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the foundling and the narrator's promise
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Fielding introduces his hero and his narrator with a wink. Notice how the narrator's asides turn the novel into a conversation. Write what the novel's claim — that a foundling's heart can outrank a gentleman's birth — meant in 1749.

name: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
teaser: Joseph Campbell's 1949 study of the monomyth — the hero's journey that recurs across every culture's myths and stories. The book that gave Hollywood its story engine and readers a map of meaning.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the call to adventure
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Campbell sets out the stages of the hero's journey. Notice how he stitches together myths from Egypt, India, and Greece. Write which stage of the journey you recognize in a story you love — and in your own life.

name: The Power of Myth
teaser: Campbell's 1988 conversations with Bill Moyers, companion to the landmark series — myth, religion, and the stories we live by, from the Star Wars galaxy to the American frontier. The most accessible door into his thought.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — myth and the modern world
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Campbell explains why myth still matters in a secular age. Notice how the conversation form keeps the ideas alive. Write what Campbell means by 'follow your bliss' — and how you would apply it.

name: The Golden Bough
teaser: James Frazer's 1890 encyclopedia of myth, magic, and religion — the ritual of the sacred grove expanded into a world survey of human belief. The book that made comparative religion a science and a story.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the king of the wood
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Frazer begins with the priest-king of Nemi and the golden bough. Notice how he accumulates examples across cultures. Write how the book's grand theory — magic giving way to religion giving way to science — still shapes how we think about belief.

name: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
teaser: Conan Doyle's 1894 second collection — The Final Problem, where Holmes and Moriarty fall together at Reichenbach Falls, plus eleven earlier cases. The volume that killed the detective and nearly killed the readership.

exploreAction.targetName: The Final Problem
exploreAction.instruction: Read The Final Problem, where Holmes faces Moriarty at the falls. Notice how the story is told by Watson after the event, with the dread of the ending already known. Write what the death of Holmes — and his return — say about how readers love a character.

name: Tales from Shakespeare
teaser: Charles and Mary Lamb's 1807 retellings of the plays in prose — the book that introduced Shakespeare to generations of children and adults who found the plays daunting. The gateway to the canon.

exploreAction.targetName: The retellings of Hamlet and The Tempest
exploreAction.instruction: Read two of the retellings. Notice how the Lambs compress the plays while keeping their feeling. Write what the collection gains and loses by turning verse into prose — and why it became the standard doorway into Shakespeare.

name: The Plague
teaser: Albert Camus's 1947 allegory of a city shut by a disease and the ordinary people — the doctor, the journalist, the exile — who choose solidarity. It has been reread in every quarantine since.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the rats and the closed gates
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the plague arrives as dead rats and a doctor's tired vigilance. Notice how Camus keeps the narration clinical even as panic grows. Write what the novel says about how ordinary people become heroes.

name: The Metamorphosis
teaser: Kafka's 1915 novella — one morning Gregor Samsa wakes as an enormous insect, and the story watches his family get on with life around him. The most famous first sentence in modern fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read the novella, noticing that no one ever asks how or why the transformation happened. Write how Kafka treats the monstrous event with total domestic realism — and what the family's relief at Gregor's death says about the book.

name: Siddhartha
teaser: Hermann Hesse's 1922 novel of a Brahmin's son who leaves asceticism, wealth, and love behind to listen to a river. A spiritual bildungsroman that found millions of readers looking for the same river.

exploreAction.targetName: The chapters about the river and the ferryman
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where Siddhartha learns from Vasudeva, the ferryman. Notice how the river teaches by being listened to rather than explained. Write what the river's laughter means — and why wisdom cannot be passed in words.

name: Steppenwolf
teaser: Hermann Hesse's 1927 novel of Harry Haller, who feels half-man, half-wolf, and is led through a Magic Theatre where every door plays with his identity. A psychedelic novel before psychedelics.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters and the Magic Theatre
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters and then the ending's Magic Theatre. Notice how Hesse dramatizes the plurality of the self. Write what the wolf represents — is it a sickness to be cured or a part to be welcomed?

name: The Magic Mountain
teaser: Thomas Mann's 1924 novel of Hans Castorp, who visits a tuberculosis sanatorium for three weeks and stays seven years, absorbing Europe's arguments about time, disease, and death before the war ends everything.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — arrival at the sanatorium
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the flatland's clock time gives way to the mountain's strange time. Notice how Mann's irony and length are part of the subject. Write how the sanatorium functions as a pressure chamber for the era.

name: The Tin Drum
teaser: Günter Grass's 1959 novel of Oskar Matzerath, who decides to stop growing at three and drums his way through Nazi Germany and beyond. A picaresque, grotesque, furious reckoning with the German past.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the decision to stop growing
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where Oskar chooses to remain a child. Notice how Grass blends fairy tale, history, and obscenity. Write what Oskar's drum and his refusal to grow say about the adults who built the world around him.

name: Perfume
teaser: Patrick Süskind's 1985 novel of Jean-Baptiste Grenouille, born with no scent of his own and gifted with perfect smell — who murders to capture the world's fragrances. A historical novel and a fable of obsession.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — birth in the fish market
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters set in 18th-century Paris, where smell is the whole sensory world. Notice how Süskind makes absence — Grenouille's missing scent — the engine. Write what the murderer's quest for a perfect perfume ultimately seeks.

name: The Reader
teaser: Bernhard Schlink's 1995 novel of a boy's affair with an older woman who is later revealed as a former camp guard. A German reckoning with guilt, illiteracy, and the generations after the Holocaust.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the affair and the readings
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Michael reads aloud to Hanna. Notice how the private ritual prefigures the public trial. Write how the novel asks what it means to love someone who did something unforgivable.

name: The Unbearable Lightness of Being
teaser: Milan Kundera's 1984 novel of love and politics in Prague — Tomas, Tereza, Sabina, and the Soviet tanks of 1968, with Nietzsche's eternal return weighing every choice. It made 'kitsch' a critical term.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the question of eternal return
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Kundera sets up the philosophical wager before the story begins. Notice how essay and narrative interleave. Write how the novel's title — lightness as burden, weight as meaning — organizes the love story.

name: Waiting for Godot
teaser: Samuel Beckett's 1953 play in which two men wait by a tree for someone who never arrives, twice. The most famous statement of the modern condition — a tragedy that plays as a comedy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening of the play and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first exchanges between Vladimir and Estragon, then the final 'Let's go / We can't / Why not / Waiting for Godot.' Notice how the repetition is the meaning. Write what waiting itself does to identity in the play.

name: The Sun Also Rises
teaser: Hemingway's 1926 novel of the lost generation — Jake Barnes, Brett Ashley, and their expatriate circle drinking and fishing and running with the bulls in Pamplona. The style changed American prose forever.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Paris and the first bullfight
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters. Notice how Hemingway's sentences are short, factual, and full of what is not said. Write what the iceberg principle (the part under water) hides in Jake and Brett's relationship, and how the prose makes you feel it.

name: The Sound and the Fury
teaser: Faulkner's 1929 novel of the Compson family told in four voices — beginning with Benjy's, who cannot tell time. A stream-of-consciousness masterpiece of decline in the American South.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Benjy's section
exploreAction.instruction: Read Benjy's section, where past and present merge through smells and events. Notice how Faulkner forces you to feel rather than follow. Write how the broken chronology itself dramatizes the family's collapse.

name: East of Eden
teaser: John Steinbeck's 1952 retelling of the Cain and Abel story in California's Salinas Valley — the Trask brothers, the Hamiltons, and a mother who owns a brothel. Steinbeck called it his big book, the one he was saving up for.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the valley and the Trask brothers
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the landscape and the family are laid out like Genesis. Notice how Steinbeck treats the word 'timshel' — the Hebrew 'thou mayest' — as the book's core. Write what the difference between must and mayest means.

name: Go Tell It on the Mountain
teaser: James Baldwin's 1953 debut novel of a boy's fourteenth birthday in a Harlem storefront church — John Grimes's crisis of faith and family, told in a voice that fused the Bible and blues into literature.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — John's Saturday and the threshing floor
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the church and the street both claim John. Notice how Baldwin's prose carries the cadence of the sermon. Write how the novel treats salvation as both promise and inheritance — what does John choose?

name: The Autobiography of Malcolm X
teaser: Malcolm X's 1965 life story, told to Alex Haley — from a Lansing childhood to Boston crime, prison study, the Nation of Islam, Mecca, and a new vision before his assassination. One of the great American testimonies.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the early years and the conk
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where young Malcolm straightens his hair and learns the rules of the street. Notice how the book is built as a conversion narrative. Write how each turning point — prison, the Nation, Mecca — transforms his understanding of himself.

name: The Wretched of the Earth
teaser: Frantz Fanon's 1961 manifesto on decolonization, written while the Algerian war burned — on violence, the colonial psychology, and the birth of a new humanity. Sartre's preface called it a cry.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapter — Concerning Violence
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapter. Notice how Fanon writes as a psychiatrist and a revolutionary at once, describing the colonial world as a compartmentalized reality. Write what he claims violence 'unbinds' in the colonized, and how you assess that claim.

name: Silent Spring
teaser: Rachel Carson's 1962 exposé of DDT and the chemical industry's assault on life — a book that began with a fable of a town where the birds fell silent and ended with the birth of environmentalism.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapter — A Fable for Tomorrow
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening fable, then a chapter on the chemistry of poisons. Notice how Carson moves from story to science to indictment. Write how she makes biochemistry urgent and readable — and what the book's legacy changed in law.

name: A Sand County Almanac
teaser: Aldo Leopold's 1949 almanac of his Wisconsin farm — month by month, from the January thaw to the December pines, ending with the land ethic that founded modern conservation thinking.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening months — January and February
exploreAction.instruction: Read the January and February chapters. Notice how Leopold turns the skunk's track and the chickadee's call into precise observation and philosophy. Write what his 'land ethic' — extending ethics to the land itself — asks of us.

name: Guns, Germs, and Steel
teaser: Jared Diamond's 1997 Pulitzer winner asking why history unfolded differently across continents — geography and biology rather than racial genius. A sweeping answer to an enormous question.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the question and the answer's shape
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Diamond frames the question of why some peoples conquered others. Notice how he insists on environmental rather than biological explanation. Write how his argument holds up as a model for asking big historical questions.

name: Nausea
teaser: Jean-Paul Sartre's 1938 novel in diary form — Roquentin in Bouville feels the world's brute existence rise in his throat. The philosophical novel that announced existentialism.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening entries and the chestnut tree scene
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening diary entries, then the famous chestnut tree passage where the root exists. Notice how Sartre turns ordinary perception into crisis. Write what 'existence precedes essence' means as Roquentin experiences it.

name: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter
teaser: Carson McCullers's 1940 debut novel of a deaf-mute man and the four townspeople — a girl, a doctor, a labor organizer, a café owner — who each pour their loneliness into him. She was 23 when she wrote it.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the cafe and the four listeners
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where each character approaches Mr. Singer with their confessions. Notice how McCullers builds a structure of parallel longings. Write why Singer, who hears nothing, becomes the confidant of a whole town.

name: The Member of the Wedding
teaser: Carson McCullers's 1946 novel of Frankie Addams, twelve years old and convinced she will join her brother's wedding and become a 'we.' A perfect portrait of the ache of adolescence.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Frankie, Berenice, and John Henry
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the kitchen conversations between Frankie and the cook Berenice carry the novel. Notice how McCullers renders the longing to belong. Write what Frankie's idea of becoming 'we' says about growing up.

name: Herzog
teaser: Saul Bellow's 1964 novel of Moses Herzog, who copes with his collapsing life by writing unsent letters to everyone — philosophers, presidents, his ex-wife. A comic masterpiece of the thinking man's breakdown.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the letter-writing begins
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Herzog's letters tumble out. Notice how Bellow's narrator is erudite, funny, and unhinged at once. Write what the letters reveal about the difference between thinking about a life and living it.

name: A Confederacy of Dunces
teaser: John Kennedy Toole's 1980 Pulitzer winner, published after his suicide — Ignatius J. Reilly, medieval scholar and slob, wages war on modern New Orleans from a hot-dog cart. One of the funniest novels ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Ignatius at the department store
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Ignatius is fired for hiding under his desk. Notice how the novel's comedy is built from his furious, erudite narration. Write how the book makes a monstrous personality endearing and even heroic.

name: The Night Circus
teaser: Erin Morgenstern's 2011 novel of a circus that appears without warning, open only at night — two young magicians bound in a lifelong duel of creation, played out in black-and-white tents.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Le Cirque des Rêves arrives
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the circus's black-and-white aesthetic and its dreamlike rules are established. Notice how Morgenstern narrates in the present tense. Write how the circus's beauty and constraint mirror the magicians' competition.

name: The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo
teaser: Taylor Jenkins Reid's 2017 novel — an aging Hollywood icon finally tells her story to an unknown journalist, and the truth about her seven marriages and the great love she hid for decades.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Evelyn's offer to Monique
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Evelyn Hugo chooses a journalist no one has heard of. Notice how the frame story sets the stakes. Write how the novel uses Hollywood glamour to hide and then reveal a story about queer love.

name: American Gods
teaser: Neil Gaiman's 2001 novel — Shadow, just out of prison, becomes the bodyguard of the mysterious Mr. Wednesday, who is gathering the old gods of America for a war against the new ones: media, money, technology.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Shadow leaves prison
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the real America — diners, motels, roadside attractions — becomes mythic. Notice how Gaiman grounds the fantastic in road-trip realism. Write what the novel says about what Americans worship now.

name: Anansi Boys
teaser: Neil Gaiman's 2005 novel — after his father's funeral, Charlie Nancy discovers he's the son of the spider god Anansi, and that his brother Spider has moved in and is ruining his life with charm.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the funeral and the discovery
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Charlie's ordinary life is invaded by myth. Notice how the book alternates comedy and menace. Write how the spider god's legacy — storytelling, trickery, songs — becomes the brothers' inheritance.

name: Guards! Guards!
teaser: Terry Pratchett's 1989 Discworld novel that introduced Sam Vimes and the City Watch — a secret society summons a dragon to take over Ankh-Morpork, and the Night Watch has to do something about it. Guards! Guards!

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Watch and the summons
