exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the Night Watch's tiny, hungover numbers are established. Notice how Pratchett builds a fantasy city that is really about policing, class, and civic decay. Write what the dragon's appearance does to the city's politics.

name: The Name of the Wind
teaser: Patrick Rothfuss's 2007 debut — Kvothe the legendary arcanist tells his own story in three days, beginning with his family of traveling performers and the night everything was taken from him.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the inn and the first day
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the innkeeper Kote is revealed as Kvothe in hiding. Notice how the frame structure promises tragedy before the adventure begins. Write how the story-within-a-story changes the reader's relation to the hero.

name: The Way of Kings
teaser: Brandon Sanderson's 2010 doorstopper, the first of the Stormlight Archive — a shattered world of highstorms and shardblades, told through a surgeon turned slave, a princess, and a captain of the dead.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the storm and Kaladin's fall
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Kaladin's enslavement is established against the world's brutal physics of storms. Notice how Sanderson builds magic systems with engineering rigor. Write how the book makes hope a kind of stubborn technology.

name: Mistborn: The Final Empire
teaser: Brandon Sanderson's 2006 debut — Vin, a street urchin, joins a crew of thieves plotting to overthrow an immortal emperor in a world of ash, using the metal-burning magic of allomancy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the skaa rebellion and Vin's discovery
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Vin's survival instincts and her magical awakening are introduced. Notice how the heist structure organizes the epic. Write how the novel makes the magic system a character in its own right.

name: Project Hail Mary
teaser: Andy Weir's 2021 novel — Ryland Grace wakes alone on a spaceship with no memory, and must solve the problem that will save Earth, with an unexpected friend he meets along the way. Hard science with a huge heart.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — waking up with amnesia
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Grace's memory loss becomes a narrative device for discovery. Notice how the mystery unfolds through reverse engineering. Write what the novel's central friendship contributes to a genre often short on warmth.

name: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
teaser: Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel that became Blade Runner — bounty hunter Rick Deckard retires androids in a radioactive San Francisco where owning a real animal is the last sign of humanity.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the sheep and the bounty
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Deckard's electric sheep introduces the novel's central anxiety. Notice how Dick uses the empathy box and the mood organ to satirize emotion. Write how the question 'what is human?' runs through every scene.

name: Being Mortal
teaser: Atul Gawande's 2014 book on aging and death — what medicine gets wrong when it treats mortality as a problem to solve instead of a life to live. A surgeon's humane study of the end.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the independence chapter
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters on the limits of independence as we age. Notice how Gawande builds argument from stories. Write what he proposes medicine should ask patients about — not just how to live longer, but how to live the life they want.

name: When Breath Becomes Air
teaser: Paul Kalanithi's 2016 memoir, finished as he died of lung cancer at 37 — a neurosurgeon's training to save lives and his own diagnosis, asking what makes a life meaningful when it ends early.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the resident and the diagnosis
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Kalanithi moves from dissecting cadavers to facing his own mortality. Notice how his medical voice never abandons him. Write what the book suggests about the difference between knowing death and knowing you will die.

name: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
teaser: Rebecca Skloot's 2010 book — Henrietta Lacks's cells, taken without consent in 1951, became the HeLa line that changed medicine, while her family never shared the fortune or the story. Science and its debt to the invisible.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the woman behind the cells
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the book moves between the lab and the Lacks family's living room. Notice how Skloot makes the science and the injustice inseparable. Write what the book says about consent, race, and who benefits from discovery.

name: The Sixth Extinction
teaser: Elizabeth Kolbert's 2014 Pulitzer winner — through frogs, corals, and great auks, she tracks the mass extinction now underway, caused by one species. A travelogue of the end of the world.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the amphibian die-off
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters on the golden frogs of Panama. Notice how Kolbert narrates extinction through fieldwork and specific species. Write how the book's structure — one extinction story per chapter — builds toward its unsettling conclusion.

name: Man's Search for Meaning
teaser: Viktor Frankl's 1946 memoir of surviving Auschwitz, and the therapy he built from it — logotherapy, the idea that the will to meaning is the deepest human drive. Part testimony, part manual for living.

exploreAction.targetName: The first part — life in the camp
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first part, where Frankl describes the camp in three psychological phases. Notice how he analyzes rather than merely recounts. Write what his claim — that meaning can be found even in suffering — asks of the reader.

name: Thinking, Fast and Slow
teaser: Daniel Kahneman's 2011 synthesis of a Nobel career — System 1 and System 2, heuristics and biases, and how our minds systematically fool us. The user manual for the human brain's bugs.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the two systems
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters introducing System 1 and System 2. Notice how Kahneman designs small experiments the reader can feel themselves failing. Write which of the book's biases you recognize in your own decisions, and why awareness alone is not enough.

name: Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow
teaser: Yuval Noah Harari's 2015 sequel — having conquered famine, plague, and war, what will humans become? Harari's answers: gods, algorithms, or obsolete. A forecast that reads like science fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the new human agenda
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Harari argues humanity now seeks immortality, bliss, and divinity. Notice how he treats futurism as history's continuation. Write how his account of 'dataism' challenges the value of individual consciousness.

name: Outliers
teaser: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book on success — the 10,000-hour rule, birth-month advantages, and the hidden cultural inheritances behind the famous. Success as accident plus inheritance plus practice.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the rule of 10,000 hours
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters on the Beatles, Bill Gates, and opportunity. Notice how Gladwell turns social science into narrative. Write what the book's emphasis on circumstance rather than talent changes about how you think about achievement.

name: The Power of Habit
teaser: Charles Duhigg's 2012 book on the science of habits — cue, routine, reward — and how individuals, companies, and movements are transformed by changing the loop. A practical theory of change.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the habit loop
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters on the habit loop and the experiments at MIT. Notice how Duhigg alternates laboratory science with corporate stories. Write how you would apply the cue-routine-reward model to a habit you want to change.

name: Deep Work
teaser: Cal Newport's 2016 book on focused attention in a distracted age — rules for the deep, undistracted concentration that produces rare and valuable work, and how to defend it from the shallow.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — deep work is valuable and rare
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Newport argues for deep work's economic and personal value. Notice how he treats attention as a finite resource. Write which of his rules — ritual, boredom, shutdown — you could actually implement this week.

name: Atomic Habits
teaser: James Clear's 2018 book on tiny changes and remarkable results — the four laws of behavior change and the compounding power of 1% improvements. A manual for becoming the person your habits are building.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the surprising power of atomic habits
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters on British cycling and the aggregation of marginal gains. Notice how Clear frames identity as the engine of habit. Write what 'every action is a vote for the type of person you wish to become' means in practice.

name: A Short History of Nearly Everything
teaser: Bill Bryson's 2003 tour of science — from the big bang to the human genome, told through the eccentric scientists who discovered it. The funniest way to learn geology, chemistry, and cosmology.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the universe and the elements
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters on the size and age of the universe. Notice how Bryson makes scale vivid through analogy. Write which discovery story in the book surprised you most, and what makes his approach to science writing work.

name: The Demon-Haunted World
teaser: Carl Sagan's 1995 defense of science and skepticism against pseudoscience — a toolkit of critical thinking from the great explainer, with the Baloney Detection Kit as its most famous gift.

exploreAction.targetName: The chapters on the Baloney Detection Kit
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where Sagan assembles his checklist for detecting flawed arguments. Notice how he applies it to both UFOs and everyday claims. Write how you would apply one of his tools to a claim you see circulating today.

name: Cosmos
teaser: Carl Sagan's 1980 companion to his landmark series — the shores of the cosmic ocean, the billion-galaxy perspective, and the pale blue dot. The book that made wonder a public service.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the shores of the cosmic ocean
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Sagan scales from a field in Ithaca to the edge of everything. Notice how he keeps the human at the center of the cosmic view. Write what the 'pale blue dot' perspective does to everyday concerns.

name: The Emperor of All Maladies
teaser: Siddhartha Mukherjee's 2010 Pulitzer-winning biography of cancer — from ancient descriptions to modern therapies, the disease as a living history of medicine, research, and hope.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the early history of cancer
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Mukherjee treats cancer as a civilization with a biography. Notice how he narrates medical history through people and experiments. Write how the book changes what you think a disease can be.

name: The Gene: An Intimate History
teaser: Siddhartha Mukherjee's 2016 book on the gene and its meanings — from Mendel to CRISPR, and the science's entanglement with his own family's history of mental illness. Genetics as biography.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Mendel and the missing heritability
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters on Mendel's peas and the rediscovery of heredity. Notice how Mukherjee keeps the science personal. Write what the book suggests about the boundary between what we inherit and what we become.

name: The Double Helix
teaser: James Watson's 1968 account of the race to discover DNA's structure — competitive, gossipy, and unapologetic, it made science look like a contact sport and remains the frankest memoir in biology.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Cambridge and the race begins
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Watson describes the rivalries and the labs. Notice how the book reads like a novel of ambition. Write what the memoir's unvarnished account adds to — and takes from — the mythology of great discovery.

name: The Selfish Gene
teaser: Richard Dawkins's 1976 book that reframed evolution from the gene's point of view — altruism as selfishness in disguise, and the 'meme' as the unit of cultural inheritance. Biology's most argued bestseller.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — why people exist
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Dawkins argues the gene is the unit of selection. Notice how the 'selfish' gene's behavior produces cooperation. Write how thinking from the gene's perspective changes the way you read altruism in everyday life.

name: Freakonomics
teaser: Steven Levitt and Stephen Dubner's 2005 book that applies economic thinking to everything — sumo wrestling, real estate agents, and the surprising causes of crime decline. The most provocative economics of its era.
byline: Steven D. Levitt and Stephen J. Dubner

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — cheating teachers and sumo wrestlers
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters on incentives and cheating. Notice how the authors treat data as a detective story. Write which of the book's conclusions most surprised you, and how incentives explain behavior you see around you.

name: Fathers and Sons
teaser: Ivan Turgenev's 1862 novel that gave the world the word 'nihilist' — the medical student Bazarov arrives to unsettle the gentry estate, and the generation gap becomes a national argument.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Bazarov's arrival
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Bazarov's rolled-up sleeves and confident denials arrive at the Kirsanov estate. Notice how Turgenev lets each generation make its case without tipping the scales. Write what nihilism meant in 1862, and whether Bazarov is consistent.

name: Resurrection
teaser: Tolstoy's 1899 late novel — a juror recognizes the accused prostitute as a woman he seduced decades before, and follows her to Siberia seeking redemption. The novel that made him a crusader for reform.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the courtroom
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Nekhlyudov sits on the jury and recognizes Katusha. Notice how Tolstoy's indictment of the justice system builds from the first page. Write how the novel's title works — who is resurrected, and into what?

name: Dead Souls
teaser: Gogol's 1842 picaresque — Chichikov travels provincial Russia buying the names of dead serfs. A comic masterpiece that flays a whole nation's vanity, greed, and emptiness.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Chichikov's arrival
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Chichikov's errand is hidden and the town's officials adore him. Notice how Gogol's grotesque humor keeps the horror close. Write what the 'dead souls' purchase says about the living souls around him.

name: Oblomov
teaser: Ivan Goncharov's 1859 novel of the man who cannot get out of bed — Oblomov's magnificent, comic, heartbreaking inertia made him a byword for the Russian national disease of dreaming.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the famous first chapter
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first chapter, where Oblomov receives visitors while lying down. Notice how Goncharov turns inaction into drama. Write what Oblomov's refusal says about his alternatives — is his inertia laziness, wisdom, or fear?

name: Lord Jim
teaser: Conrad's 1900 novel of a young officer who jumps from a sinking ship and spends his life trying to prove he is not a coward — a deep-sea dive into honor, guilt, and second chances.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Patna and the jump
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Jim's moment of decision arrives and passes. Notice how Marlow narrates Jim's story through layers of testimony. Write what the novel suggests about whether one act can define a life.

name: The Turn of the Screw
teaser: Henry James's 1898 ghost story — a governess at Bly is convinced the children are possessed by the dead servants. Is she seeing ghosts or losing her mind? The most argued ambiguity in English fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the governess arrives at Bly
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the governess's excitement curdles into dread. Notice how James withholds certainty about what is real. Write which reading you favor — ghosts, madness, or something else — and what evidence tips you.

name: The Portrait of a Lady
teaser: Henry James's 1881 novel of Isabel Archer, an American woman of bright independence who chooses badly and stays — a study of freedom, money, and the traps set by people who love you.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Isabel's arrival in England
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Isabel's intelligence and her illusions are both established. Notice how James tracks her choices with ironic sympathy. Write what the novel suggests about the freedom to make one's own life — and its costs.

name: Pygmalion
teaser: George Bernard Shaw's 1913 play of Professor Higgins's bet that he can pass a flower girl off as a duchess — the sharpest comedy ever written about class, speech, and who gets to belong.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening acts — Covent Garden and the bet
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening acts, where Eliza's accent marks her as fair game. Notice how Shaw's preface and stage directions carry his argument. Write what the play says about language as class passport — and why Shaw insisted Eliza does not marry Higgins.

name: The Importance of Being Earnest
teaser: Oscar Wilde's 1895 comedy of two young men who invent a friend named Bunbury and a name named Ernest — the most perfectly constructed farce in English, glittering with epigrams.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening act — Algernon and the cucumber sandwiches
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening act, where Ernest, Bunbury, and the cucumber sandwiches establish the play's logic of elegant deceit. Notice how every line works toward the final revelation. Write what the play's obsession with being 'earnest' is really satirizing.

name: On the Road
teaser: Jack Kerouac's 1957 novel of Sal Paradise and Dean Moriarty crossing America in stolen cars and borrowed time — the Beat generation's declaration of independence, written in one long jazz riff.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the first road trip west
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the road itself becomes the narrator. Notice how Kerouac's prose runs without brakes, sentence after sentence. Write what the book offers that a settled life cannot, and what it costs its characters.

name: Naked Lunch
teaser: William S. Burroughs's 1959 cut-up novel — a hallucinated travelogue of addiction, control, and the Interzone, assembled from fragments and banned in Boston. It made the avant-garde a legal battleground.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening sections — the market and the mugwump
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening sections. Notice how Burroughs's prose shifts registers without warning, mixing clinical horror and vaudeville. Write what the book's fragmentary form has to do with its subject — addiction as a control system.

name: A Canticle for Leibowitz
teaser: Walter M. Miller Jr.'s 1959 novel across a thousand years after nuclear war — the monks of the Order of Leibowitz preserve the scraps of the old world, including the blueprint for its destruction. The great Catholic science-fiction novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Brother Francis and the memorabilia
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Brother Francis finds the blessed blueprint. Notice how Miller treats the preservation of knowledge with both reverence and irony. Write what the novel says about whether humanity can learn from its own history.

name: The Last Unicorn
teaser: Peter S. Beagle's 1968 novel of the unicorn who leaves her wood to find the others — through Schmendrick the magician and Molly Grue, into the Red Bull's country. The most lyrical fantasy novel ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the unicorn leaves the wood
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the unicorn's immortality meets her loneliness. Notice how Beagle's prose is precise and sorrowful at once. Write what it means to the unicorn to become human in the course of the quest.

name: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe
teaser: C. S. Lewis's 1950 first Narnia book — four children step through a wardrobe into a land of eternal winter, a White Witch, and a lion who is not safe but is good. The most beloved portal fantasy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Lucy and the wardrobe
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Lucy's discovery of the wardrobe is met with disbelief. Notice how Lewis lets the children's argument play out in the ordinary world first. Write how the novel's Christian allegory works — and how it works for non-Christians too.

name: The Hobbit
teaser: J. R. R. Tolkien's 1937 novel of Bilbo Baggins, thirteen dwarves, and a dragon — a burglar who did not know he was a burglar, written first for Tolkien's own children. The door into Middle-earth.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — An Unexpected Party
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapter, where the dwarves arrive one by one and the adventure begins against Bilbo's will. Notice how Tolkien's narrator keeps breaking in with asides. Write how Bilbo's growth — from comfort to courage — is the book's quiet engine.

name: The Princess Bride
teaser: William Goldman's 1973 novel of true love, fencing, giants, and ROUSes — presented as the good parts of a classic by 'S. Morgenstern.' The funniest book about storytelling ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the grandfather's frame and the princess's birth
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Goldman's invented editor interrupts the story. Notice how the frame makes the reader both child and adult. Write what the novel's claim — that this is only the 'good parts' — reveals about how stories work.

name: Watership Down
teaser: Richard Adams's 1972 novel of rabbits who leave their doomed warren and cross the English downs toward a promised hill — an adventure epic, a survival story, and a meditation on freedom, told with rabbits' own mythology.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Fiver's vision and the flight
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Fiver's dread and Hazel's courage set the quest in motion. Notice how Adams builds a complete rabbit culture with its own language and legends. Write what the novel says about freedom, leadership, and the courage to leave.

name: The Tombs of Atuan
teaser: Le Guin's 1971 second Earthsea novel — Tenar, the priestess of the Nameless Ones, guards the tombs in darkness until a wizard comes to steal the ring and offers her a way out. The fantasy of freedom from within.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Tenar's consecration and the dark place
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Tenar's life is given to the dark before she understands what she has lost. Notice how Le Guin renders the tombs' horror in the child's own terms. Write what Tenar must choose between, and what freedom costs her.

name: The Faraway Tree and the Folk of the Faraway Tree
teaser: Enid Blyton's magical tree that reaches into new lands each week — Moon-Face, Silky, and the Saucepan Man at the top of the ladder. The books that taught generations of children to climb.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the discovery of the tree
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the children find the tree and its peculiar residents. Notice how Blyton keeps the wonder concrete — the lands change weekly, and the food is always at the top. Write what makes a children's fantasy of pure abundance so enduring.

name: Hamlet
teaser: Shakespeare's tragedy of the prince who cannot act — revenge delayed until it is too late, and the most quoted play in the language. Four centuries of readers still arguing about what Hamlet wants.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One and the 'To be or not to be' soliloquy
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, where the ghost sets the task, then the famous soliloquy. Notice how Shakespeare lets Hamlet's questions expand beyond revenge. Write what the play suggests about action, thought, and the cost of either.

name: Macbeth
teaser: Shakespeare's shortest tragedy and his darkest — the thane who takes the witches' word and murders his way to a crown he cannot keep. A study of ambition, blood, and the imagination that feeds both.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One and the dagger soliloquy
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, from the witches to the murder. Notice how the play compresses time and consequence. Write what the floating dagger means — is Macbeth's tragedy ambition, weakness, or the imagination itself?

name: King Lear
teaser: Shakespeare's storm play — the king who divides his kingdom by flattery and is stripped to nothing on a heath in the rain. The most harrowing tragedy in the language, and the most forgiving in its last scene.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One and the heath scenes in Act Three
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, where Lear's rage dismembers his family, then the heath scenes, where the king meets the naked beggar. Notice how the storm is both weather and mind. Write what Lear learns on the heath that he could not learn on the throne.

name: Romeo and Juliet
teaser: Shakespeare's early tragedy of the star-crossed lovers of Verona — a comedy that turns, at the interval, into the most famous disaster in literature. The archetype of forbidden love.

exploreAction.targetName: The balcony scene and the final act
exploreAction.instruction: Read the balcony scene, then the final act, where the timing of a letter decides everything. Notice how Shakespeare compresses the lovers' whole romance into a few days. Write what the play says about the speed of youth and the slowness of adults.

name: Beowulf
teaser: The Old English epic of the Geatish hero who kills Grendel, Grendel's mother, and finally the dragon — a poem about glory, age, and the kingdom that ends when its king falls.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening and the dragon's final battle
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening, where the poem begins with a funeral and promises another, then the dragon fight. Notice how the scop's elegiac voice carries the whole poem. Write what Beowulf's three monsters have in common, and what the poem says about fame after death.

name: The Ramayana
teaser: Valmiki's ancient Sanskrit epic of Rama, his exile, the abduction of Sita, and the war to win her back with the help of Hanuman — India's great poem of duty, love, and righteousness.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening books — the exile and the abduction
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening books, where Rama accepts exile without protest and Sita is taken. Notice how the epic's moral order — dharma — shapes every choice. Write how the poem treats duty versus desire, and why Rama's perfection still stirs argument.

name: The Mahabharata
teaser: The great Indian epic of the war between the Pandavas and the Kauravas — containing the Bhagavad Gita, and every story India ever told. Longer than the Iliad and Odyssey combined, and deeper.

exploreAction.targetName: The Bhagavad Gita, chapters 1–2, within the epic
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of the Gita, where Arjuna despairs before the battle and Krishna counsels him. Notice how the epic pauses its war for philosophy. Write what Krishna's teaching about duty, desire, and detachment means in the face of an actual war.

name: The Thousand and One Nights
teaser: The Arabian collection of tales told by Scheherazade to postpone her execution — Sinbad, Ali Baba, Aladdin, and stories nested inside stories. The frame tale that invented storytelling as survival.

exploreAction.targetName: The frame — the king and Scheherazade — and one tale
exploreAction.instruction: Read the frame story and a tale like The Fisherman and the Jinni. Notice how each story must end unfinished to buy another night. Write how the frame makes narrative itself a matter of life and death, and what that says about why we tell stories.

name: Journey to the West
teaser: The Chinese classic of the monk Tripitaka's pilgrimage to India, guarded by the Monkey King, Pigsy, and Sandy — part adventure, part satire, part spiritual allegory. The source of Dragon Ball and much else.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Monkey King's rebellion
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the stone monkey declares himself equal to heaven. Notice how the novel blends chaos, comedy, and quest. Write what the Monkey King represents, and why the pilgrimage needs such a wild guard.

name: The Tale of Genji
teaser: Murasaki Shikibu's 11th-century novel of the shining prince and the court of Heian Japan — often called the world's first novel. Courtly love, poetry, and the melancholy beauty of a closed world.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Genji's birth and early loves
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Genji's beauty and his forbidden love for his father's consort are established. Notice how the novel's tone — elegant, wistful, oblique — carries its morality. Write how the Heian court's aesthetics shape its ethics.

name: Love in the Time of Cholera
teaser: García Márquez's 1985 novel of Florentino Ariza, who waits fifty-one years, nine months, and four days to love Fermina Daza again — a novel about love as persistence, and the river journey that ends it.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the death and the return
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the doctor dies on Pentecost Sunday and Florentino declares his century-old love. Notice how García Márquez treats love as both sickness and art. Write what the novel says about loving the same person across a lifetime.

name: Pedro Páramo
teaser: Juan Rulfo's 1955 novel of Juan Preciado, who travels to Comala to find his father and finds a town of the dead instead — a hundred and twenty pages that changed Latin American fiction forever.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the journey to Comala
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the dead speak and the living narrator is already lost. Notice how Rulfo's fragmented voices build the town's whole history. Write how the novel treats death, memory, and the weight of a father's name.

name: Hopscotch
teaser: Julio Cortázar's 1963 experimental novel that invites you to skip chapters — the story of Horacio Oliveira in Paris and Buenos Aires, with 'expendable chapters' you may read in a second order. A novel as a game.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters and the reader's table of instructions
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters and the table of instructions that offers two ways to read. Notice how Cortázar makes the reader part of the fiction. Write how the alternative reading orders change the meaning of the same scenes.

name: The Invention of Morel
teaser: Adolfo Bioy Casares's 1940 novel of a castaway on a deserted island who discovers a machine that replays the past — and falls in love with a ghost. Borges called it flawless.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the journal and the visitors
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the castaway's journal decodes the island's impossible visitors. Notice how Bioy Casares keeps the mystery rigorously logical. Write how the novel uses science fiction to ask what it means to love someone who is an image.

name: Of Mice and Men
teaser: Steinbeck's 1937 novella of George and Lennie, who carry their dream of a farm from ranch to ranch — a small perfect tragedy about friendship, strength, and the tenderness that destroys.

exploreAction.targetName: The full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read the novella, from the clearing where the story opens and closes. Notice how Steinbeck builds the dream of the farm to make the ending land harder. Write what George's final act costs him, and what the novella says about mercy.

name: Cannery Row
teaser: Steinbeck's 1945 comic novel of the Monterey sardine street — Doc, Mack and the boys, and a party for a man who helps everyone. A celebration of the useless, generous, and broke.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the street and its characters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Steinbeck introduces the street as a character. Notice how he treats the community's plans and failures with affection. Write what Cannery Row proposes about success, purpose, and friendship.

name: My Ántonia
teaser: Willa Cather's 1918 novel of the Nebraska prairie and the immigrant girl Ántonia Shimerda — Jim Burden's memory of a childhood friendship that becomes the measure of his life. The great American pastoral.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the journey to Nebraska
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Jim and Ántonia arrive on the prairie as children. Notice how Cather renders the land as both harsh and holy. Write what Ántonia comes to mean to Jim — and why he calls her story his own.

name: Death Comes for the Archbishop
teaser: Willa Cather's 1927 novel of two French priests building a diocese across the desert Southwest — a saint's life, a travelogue, and a meditation on how place shapes a soul.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the bishop's journey
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Bishop Latour rides through a landscape older than his church. Notice how Cather slows time to the pace of the desert. Write how the novel's episodic structure mirrors the life it honors.

name: The Bridge of San Luis Rey
teaser: Thornton Wilder's 1927 Pulitzer-winning novella — when a Peruvian bridge collapses and five people fall, a friar investigates why God chose those five. A small perfect book about love and chance.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters and the final chapter
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening, where the bridge falls and the investigation begins, then the closing meditation. Notice how Wilder weaves the five lives together. Write what the novel concludes about the 'why' the friar seeks — and whether an answer is possible.

name: Our Town
teaser: Thornton Wilder's 1938 play of Grover's Corners, New Hampshire — the milkman, the choir, the wedding, and the graveyard. A play that makes an ordinary life feel like the greatest mystery there is.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One and Act Three
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, where the Stage Manager introduces the town, then Act Three, where Emily returns to one ordinary day. Notice how the play's minimal staging forces attention onto the words. Write what 'Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?' asks of you.

name: Ethan Frome
teaser: Edith Wharton's 1911 novella of a Massachusetts farm, a sick wife, a young cousin, and one sled ride — a tragedy of the poor and silent, framed by the narrator who pieces together what happened.

exploreAction.targetName: The full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read the novella, from the frame narrator's arrival in Starkfield to the sled ride's aftermath. Notice how Wharton builds the snow and the silence. Write what the smash-up costs each of the three, and why the story needs its frame.

name: The Age of Innocence
teaser: Edith Wharton's 1920 Pulitzer-winning novel of Newland Archer and the Countess Olenska in old New York — a society that punishes scandal while pretending to be innocent. The great novel of manners.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the opera and the engagement
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the opera box and the engagement announce the rules of Newland's world. Notice how Wharton narrates what cannot be said. Write what the novel says about the freedom that comes too late.

name: The Awakening
teaser: Kate Chopin's 1899 novel of Edna Pontellier, who wakes to her own desires in the summer heat of Grand Isle — and cannot fit back into the life that waits. The novel that scandalized and then defined an era.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the summer at Grand Isle
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Edna's awakening begins in the sea and the music. Notice how Chopin links the ocean with the self. Write what the final swim means — is it defeat, triumph, or something that is neither?

name: Maggie: A Girl of the Streets
teaser: Stephen Crane's 1893 novella of the Bowery — a girl, a brother, a neighborhood, and a fall written with the cold precision of a newspaper report. American naturalism's opening document.

exploreAction.targetName: The full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read the novella, from the tenement childhood to the ending. Notice how Crane reports Maggie's tragedy without sentiment. Write what the novel's refusal to moralize achieves, and how its irony indicts the neighborhood that made it.

name: Sister Carrie
teaser: Theodore Dreiser's 1900 novel of Carrie Meeber, who arrives in Chicago with a trunk and rises — while the man who loves her falls. American naturalism's big-city epic of desire and drift.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the train to Chicago
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Carrie's arrival and her first disappointment are rendered with documentary exactness. Notice how Dreiser treats ambition as weather. Write what the novel suggests about luck, want, and the machinery of the city.

name: The Jungle
teaser: Upton Sinclair's 1906 novel of the Lithuanian immigrant Jurgis Rudkus in Chicago's meatpacking yards — the novel that made America change its food laws. Socialism, slaughter, and a family eaten alive.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the wedding and the yards
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the wedding feast and the packinghouse set Jurgis's hopes and their end. Notice how Sinclair piles fact on fact to indict the system. Write how the novel's reformist argument works through one family's ruin.

name: Progress and Poverty
teaser: Henry George's 1879 treatise asking why poverty grows alongside progress — and proposing the single tax on land. A book that moved millions and shaped labor, land, and urban policy worldwide.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the riddle of poverty amid progress
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where George states the paradox the book will answer. Notice how he argues in plain, forceful prose. Write what his diagnosis — that land speculation captures the gains of growth — suggests about cities today.

name: Up from Slavery
teaser: Booker T. Washington's 1901 autobiography — from a Virginia slave cabin to founding Tuskegee Institute — a self-help epic and one of the most influential and contested books in Black American history.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — slavery and freedom
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Washington describes emancipation and his hunger for education. Notice how he frames progress as gradual and practical. Write how his philosophy of accommodation was both praised and fiercely criticized by his contemporaries.

name: The Souls of Black Folk
teaser: W. E. B. Du Bois's 1903 collection of essays that gave the world 'double consciousness' and the color line — part sociology, part memoir, part hymn. The founding text of modern Black thought.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — of our spiritual strivings
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapter, where Du Bois describes the veil and double consciousness. Notice how he blends history, statistics, and personal testimony. Write what 'two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings' means, and whether the problem he names has changed.

name: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
teaser: Douglass's 1845 memoir of his enslavement and escape — the whip, the learning to read, the fight with Covey — written to prove he was a man, and the most powerful American testimony of its century.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — learning to read
exploreAction.instruction: Read the chapters where Douglass is taught letters and then forbidden them. Notice how he narrates the growth of his own mind under slavery. Write what the book says about literacy as freedom, and how the fight with Covey turns him into a man.

name: Uncle Tom's Cabin
teaser: Harriet Beecher Stowe's 1852 novel that Lincoln reportedly greeted as the cause of the Civil War — the sentimental epic of Tom, Eliza, and the fugitives. The most consequential novel in American history.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the sale and Eliza's flight
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Tom is sold down the river and Eliza crosses the ice with her child. Notice how Stowe uses the reader's sympathy as a political weapon. Write how the novel's sentimentality both moved history and has since been complicated.

name: Little House on the Prairie
teaser: Laura Ingalls Wilder's 1935 novel of the Ingalls family's covered-wagon year on the Kansas prairie — the second book of the series that made pioneer childhood a national memory.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the journey west
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the family crosses rivers and builds a house of logs. Notice how Wilder renders the prairie through a child's senses. Write what the book preserves — and what it quietly leaves out — about westward expansion.

name: Tarzan of the Apes
teaser: Edgar Rice Burroughs's 1912 novel of the English lord raised by apes in the African jungle — the adventure that became a century of movies, comics, and arguments. Read as pure myth, it still moves.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the cabin and the apes
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the infant Tarzan is orphaned and adopted. Notice how Burroughs narrates the boy's education in the jungle with relish. Write how the novel's premise — nature versus nurture — made it so durable, and so contested.

name: The Dark Forest
teaser: Liu Cixin's 2008 second volume of the Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy — humanity prepares for an alien invasion centuries away, and a man must decide whether the universe is a forest of hunters.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the wallfacers
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the wallfacers are chosen to deceive the enemy by deceiving everyone. Notice how Liu Cixin thinks at the scale of centuries. Write what the 'dark forest' theory claims about contact between civilizations.

name: Ball Lightning
teaser: Liu Cixin's 2004 novel of a scientist obsessed with the mystery his parents were killed by — ball lightning — and the weapon it can become. Hard SF about the strange marriage of weather and war.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the storm and the obsession
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Chen's parents vanish in a lightning strike and his life's question is set. Notice how Liu Cixin grounds cosmic speculation in precise physics. Write how the novel uses an unexplained phenomenon to explore obsession and sacrifice.

name: Solaris
teaser: Stanisław Lem's 1961 novel of a scientist sent to a station above the ocean planet Solaris — where the ocean's contact takes the shape of your deepest guilt. The great novel of unknowable otherness.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Kelvin's arrival
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Kelvin arrives at the station and the strange visitors are already there. Notice how Lem refuses to explain the ocean away. Write what the novel suggests about the limits of understanding — and whether contact is possible at all.

name: The Dispossessed
teaser: Le Guin's 1974 novel of Shevek, a physicist from the anarchist moon Anarres who travels to the capitalist planet Urras — 'an ambiguous utopia' that questions both worlds. The novel that made 'anarchist' a literary ideal.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Anarres and the wall
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Shevek's departure from Anarres is narrated against memories of his utopia. Notice how Le Guin structures the novel in alternating worlds. Write what the novel says about freedom, solidarity, and the walls we build.

name: The Martian Chronicles
teaser: Bradbury's 1950 linked story cycle of the colonization of Mars — a bittersweet mirror held up to Earth, where the Martians die of chicken pox and the humans bring their own doom. The prose is pure poetry.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening stories — the rockets and the Martians
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening stories, from the rockets to the Martians' last telepathic moments. Notice how Bradbury treats Mars as a state of mind. Write how the collection uses the frontier to comment on Earth's own history.

name: Rendezvous with Rama
teaser: Clarke's 1973 novel of an alien cylinder entering the solar system — a first-contact story with no contact, a mystery with no answer. Hard SF's most elegant demonstration of wonder without explanation.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the detection of Rama
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where humanity watches Rama's approach with growing awe. Notice how Clarke makes the reader feel the scale of the artifact. Write what the novel gains by never explaining who built Rama or why.

name: Brave New World Revisited
teaser: Huxley's 1958 nonfiction sequel — written thirty years after his novel, he examines the actual techniques of control: propaganda, drugs, and the 'managed democracy' he feared more than Orwell's totalitarian state.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the prophecy and its tools
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Huxley compares his own predictions with the world of 1958. Notice how he updates his fictional warnings with real politics and psychology. Write which of his control techniques you see most clearly in your own media diet.

name: Going Postal
teaser: Terry Pratchett's 2004 Discworld novel of Moist von Lipwig, a con man given a choice — run the post office or die — who discovers that running a failing institution is the greatest con of all.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the hanging and the offer
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Moist's 'execution' becomes a job offer. Notice how Pratchett builds comedy out of institutional absurdity. Write what the novel says about bureaucracy, communication, and the art of making things work.

name: Small Gods
teaser: Pratchett's 1992 Discworld novel of Brutha, the only believer left in the god Om — who has been reduced to a tortoise. A novel about faith, institutions, and what happens when belief becomes bureaucracy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the tortoise and the novice
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Om the tortoise and Brutha the simple novice meet. Notice how Pratchett uses the size of the god as a joke with theology inside it. Write what the novel says about the difference between religion and belief.

name: Norse Mythology
teaser: Neil Gaiman's 2017 retelling of the Norse myths — Odin, Thor, and Loki from the creation to Ragnarök, told in a storyteller's voice that makes the old gods feel like old friends.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the creation and the mead
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, from the void Ginnungagap to the building of Asgard. Notice how Gaiman keeps the myths episodic and wry. Write what the Norse gods' flaws — Loki's tricks, Thor's temper — reveal about what these myths were for.

name: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
teaser: Gaiman's 2013 novella of a man who returns to his childhood home and remembers the girl at the end of the lane, the monsters, and the ocean that was really there. Memory as the deepest fantasy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the return and the lane
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the narrator's return unlocks the past. Notice how Gaiman keeps the adult and child narrators in the same breath. Write what the ocean at the end of the lane is, and what the book says about childhood's magic.

name: The Graveyard Book
teaser: Gaiman's 2008 Newbery-winning novel of Nobody Owens, raised by the dead in a graveyard after his family is murdered — a coming-of-age story where the ghosts are the best parents. The Jungle Book with tombstones.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Nobody and the man Jack
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the toddler escapes the murderer and is adopted by the graveyard. Notice how Gaiman makes the dead warm and the living threatening. Write how the book uses the graveyard's lessons — history, silence, mortality — to raise a child.

name: Hogfather
teaser: Pratchett's 1996 Discworld novel — with the Hogfather missing, Death must take his place and deliver the toys, while Susan tries to save the sun from being switched off. A novel about belief, from the most beloved of fantasy satirists.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the assassins and the list
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the plot to kill the Hogfather is set in motion. Notice how Pratchett wraps serious questions about belief in slapstick. Write what the book's famous lines — about how humans need fantasy to stay human — mean to you.

name: Assassin's Apprentice
teaser: Robin Hobb's 1995 first novel of the Realm of the Elderlings — Fitz, a royal bastard trained as an assassin and bonded to a wolf, in a kingdom of scheming courtiers. The fantasy of quiet, painful intimacy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the boy left at the keep
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the six-year-old Fitz is abandoned at Buckkeep. Notice how Hobb narrates from inside Fitz's wounded, watchful perspective. Write how the novel builds its magic — the Skill and the Wit — around loneliness and loyalty.

name: Gideon the Ninth
teaser: Tamsyn Muir's 2019 novel of necromancers, a locked-tomb trial, and Gideon Nav — a swordswoman who would rather be anywhere else. Lesbian necromancers in space, with a voice like a meme and a heart like a gothic novel.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Ninth House and the invitation
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Gideon's escape plans keep failing and the Emperor's summons arrives. Notice how Muir balances snark and gothic grandeur. Write how the novel's outrageous premise becomes genuinely moving by the end.

name: All Systems Red
teaser: Martha Wells's 2017 first Murderbot novella — a self-hacking security android that would rather watch media than protect its clients, until it decides to anyway. The most beloved robot in modern science fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the survey team and the murderbot
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Murderbot's deadpan narration introduces its media habit and its job. Notice how Wells makes the reader care about a character who insists it doesn't care. Write what Murderbot's name — and its refusal to be called a 'SecUnit' — reveals.

name: Heaven
teaser: Mieko Kawakami's 2009 novel about a 14-year-old boy with a lazy eye who is bullied daily, until a girl named Kojima — the class's other outcast — starts leaving him anonymous notes. Their secret friendship becomes the only place either of them feels human.

exploreAction.targetName: Heaven — the opening chapters and the Whale Park meeting
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening — the boy discovers the first note in his pencil case. Then read the Whale Park scene where Kojima reveals herself. Notice how Kawakami builds an entire world out of two outcasts passing paper. The novel's quiet violence works because you're reading it from inside the victim's head.

synopsis:
Set in a Japanese middle school in 1991, Heaven follows an unnamed 14-year-old boy whose lazy eye — one eye aims in a different direction from the other — makes him a constant target. Classmates call him "Ronpari" (one eye on London, one on Paris) and beat him routinely. His home life offers no refuge: a distant mother, an absent father, and the quiet shame of a household that doesn't ask questions.

The cruelty is specific and methodical. Ninomiya, the class's top student, orchestrates the worst of it; his friend Momose delivers the philosophy behind it — people hurt each other because they can, and there is no deeper reason. The boy absorbs this nihilism until a note appears in his pencil case: "We should be friends." The handwriting is delicate, unsigned.

The notes lead him to Kojima, a girl his age who is shunned for her dirty clothes, unkempt hair, and the smell the other students mock. She goes by "Hazmat." Her mother left her father for a wealthier man, and Kojima — who loved her father — stopped bathing as a way of holding on to him. She believes her suffering purifies her, a conviction the novel treats with both sympathy and alarm.

Their friendship exists only in letters, hidden in desks and read in bathrooms. Through them they build a private world — sharing hobbies, small observations, fragments of who they might be if the world weren't hostile. The act of writing becomes the only time either of them speaks honestly.

The bullying escalates. A sadistic gymnasium game leaves the boy bloodied and cleaning his own mess while Kojima watches in silence. She argues that their refusal to fight back is not cowardice but a form of resistance — a way of refusing to become what the bullies expect. The boy is unconvinced but can't articulate why.

He is offered surgery to correct his lazy eye — a chance to look normal, to disappear into the crowd. Kojima reacts with anguish, calling it a betrayal of everything their friendship means. Their bond fractures under the weight of this choice. He stops writing. She stops eating.

Months later, a letter arrives. Meet me at Whale Park — the neglected playground where they first spoke. When they arrive, Ninomiya and his friends are waiting. The bullies demand a public humiliation. In a final act of defiance, Kojima strips naked and confronts them, laughing until they flee in horror. Adults arrive. Kojima is taken away. The boy never sees her again.

In the aftermath, the boy tells his mother everything — the first time he has spoken the truth. He gets the surgery. Afterward, the world sharpens into something almost unbearable in its beauty. He thinks of Kojima often, carrying the weight of what they shared and what was taken from them.

Kawakami wrote the novel after reading Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, and the influence shows: the book is less about bullying than about whether suffering can mean anything at all. Kojima says yes. Momose says no. The boy, caught between them, spends the novel trying to find his own answer. The Murasaki Shikibu Prize committee recognized it in 2010; the English translation by Sam Bett and David Boyd was shortlisted for the International Booker Prize in 2022.

chapters.title: The First Note
chapters.summary: The narrator introduces his daily life of bullying — beatings, name-calling, the isolation of having a lazy eye. A mysterious note appears in his pencil case: "We should be friends."

chapters.title: Whale Park
chapters.summary: The note leads to a meeting at Whale Park, a neglected playground. Kojima — the class's other outcast, mocked as "Hazmat" — reveals herself as the writer. Their first real conversation begins.

chapters.title: Letters in Hiding
chapters.summary: The boy and Kojima begin exchanging letters secretly — hidden in desks, read in bathrooms. Their notes become a lifeline, a private world where they can speak honestly about everything except their pain.

chapters.title: Signs and Scissors
chapters.summary: Kojima reveals her ritual of cutting objects in the classroom — not destruction but control. She explains her "signs": the dirty clothes, the unwashed hair, all ways of preserving her connection to her absent father.

chapters.title: Heaven
chapters.summary: Summer vacation. Kojima takes the boy to an art museum she calls "Heaven" — a painting of two lovers finding peace after suffering. The day is the novel's single moment of freedom. She cries silently on a bench. He offers her his hair to cut.

chapters.title: The Return of Violence
chapters.summary: School resumes and the bullying intensifies. A gymnasium ordeal — a sadistic "human soccer" game — leaves the boy bloodied. Kojima helps him clean up. She argues their refusal to fight back is resistance, not weakness.

chapters.title: Momose
chapters.summary: Outside school, the boy confronts Momose — Ninomiya's philosophical lieutenant. Momose delivers a chilling worldview: people act only on desire, there is no inherent meaning, the strong dominate the weak. The boy is shaken.

chapters.title: The Choice
chapters.summary: The boy is offered surgery to correct his lazy eye. Kojima sees it as betrayal — an attempt to escape their shared identity. Their friendship fractures. He stops writing. She stops eating.

chapters.title: The Final Letter
chapters.summary: After months of silence, Kojima sends one last letter: meet at Whale Park. When they arrive, the bullies are waiting. In a final act of defiance, Kojima strips and confronts them. Adults arrive. She is taken away. The boy never sees her again.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: The boy tells his mother everything for the first time. He gets the surgery. The world sharpens into beauty. He carries Kojima's memory — what they shared, what was lost — into a life that continues, changed.
